notation.meaning: Natural rate of unemployment: the rate the economy returns to in the long run
Potential output: output consistent with the natural rate
Slope: how strongly inflation responds to the gap
Intercept of the traditional curve (here not the IS slope)

blocks.md: When the economy runs hot, with output above what it can normally sustain, firms struggle to find workers and raise wages and prices faster, so inflation rises. When it runs cold, inflation falls. The first versions of this idea promised a stable menu: accept more inflation and get permanently lower unemployment. That broke down in the 1970s, when inflation and unemployment rose together. The fix was to add expectations: what pushes inflation up is not a strong economy as such, but a strong economy relative to what people already expect inflation to be. Supply shocks, such as an oil price jump, push inflation up on top.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the supply side of modern short-run models: the link from the output gap to inflation that central banks must manage.
The traditional Phillips curve relates inflation to unemployment, $\pi_t = \alpha - \gamma u_t$. The **expectations-augmented** version uses deviations from expectations and the natural rate,
and, replacing unemployment with output, with an aggregate supply shock:
When expected inflation rises, the whole curve shifts up: the same unemployment rate comes with higher inflation, which is what the data of the 1970s showed.

| Version | Relationship | Origin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Traditional | Wage growth (later price inflation) falls with unemployment | Phillips (1958), UK data; Samuelson and Solow, US 1960s |
| Breakdown | Inflation and unemployment rose together in the 1970s and 1980s | — |
| Expectations-augmented | Only inflation *surprises* move with unemployment | Friedman and Phelps |

sections.heading: The Phillips curve as a policy menu

blocks.md: Samuelson and Solow (1960) replicated Phillips's relationship on US data and presented it as a "menu of choice" for policy: lower unemployment could be bought with higher inflation (in their figure, roughly 3% unemployment with 4–5% inflation, or price stability with 5–6% unemployment). Friedman and Phelps argued instead that the economy returns to a **natural rate of unemployment** in the long run — the rate "ground out by the Walrasian system of general equilibrium equations" given the structure of the labor and goods markets — so higher inflation lowers unemployment only until expectations adjust. Trying to exploit the menu shifts the curve: an instance of the [Lucas Critique](note:lucas-critique).

blocks.md: With $\pi^e_t = 2$, $\gamma = 1$ and $y^* = 100$: at $y_t = 99$ and no shock, $\pi_t = 2 + (99 - 100) = 1$; a supply shock $\epsilon^\pi_t = 3$ at the same output gives $\pi_t = 4$.

- **Treating it as a menu.** Higher inflation buys lower unemployment only while it is unexpected; once $\pi^e$ catches up, the gap closes.
- **Sign of the slope.** In unemployment the slope is negative ($-\gamma$); in output it is positive ($+\gamma$).
- **Shocks.** $\epsilon^\pi$ raises inflation at every level of output: a supply shock shifts the curve up.
- Macro: the supply block of the [IS-MP-PC Model](note:is-mp-pc-model) and of New Keynesian models; inflation forecasting.
